The complete draft collection is available for review. See the new draft collection . A relational database stores related facts in tables: rows of values under named columns. It answers questions about them and applies changes under specified rules. A shop can ask which customer placed an order, what that order contains and whether it has been paid. It can also make “record the order and take the stock” one complete change, even while other customers are buying. The tables are only part of the bargain. You choose what a row means, which invalid facts the database must refuse and how competing changes make their decisions. The application must handle interrupted requests; somebody must keep recoverable copies. Understanding those boundaries is what makes a relational database useful beyond storing a spreadsheet on a server. Follow one small shop selling tea and tea things. Mina Shah places order 103 for one blue mug and two packets of green tea. It costs £29.00. There is only one mug left, and Tariq Aziz is trying to buy it too. We will give those facts a home, calculate an answer, protect the purchase and follow it through failure. The shop and figures are illustrative; the query results and competing-update outcomes were checked on PostgreSQL 18.6. Investigate a correctness incident. Making concurrent changes correct turns a forbidden outcome and two overlapping requests into a protocol you can test. Explain a slow workload. Understanding and improving database performance finds where work and waiting accumulate, then checks a specific improvement. Prepare for failure. Running a relational service turns acceptable loss and interruption into an owned, rehearsed recovery procedure. Evaluate a system. Start with the shortlist below . Follow the distribution question if location, failure survival or write capacity requires several servers. Give each fact a home Ask for an answer and check its shape Reserve the last mug Follow the work behind the statement Complete the application request Recover the right state Put data and decisions in the right place Choose a system you can test Give each fact a home A table represents one kind of fact. Each row is an instance of that fact; named columns hold its values. A row in customers describes one customer. A row in orders describes one placed order. A row in order_items describes one numbered line within an order, which we will call an order line . The relational model calls a table-shaped collection of facts a relation . Its useful promise here is that facts have explicit identities and can be combined through matching values. You need not pack every fact shown on a screen into one stored row. A primary key is the column or columns chosen to identify each row uniquely, with no missing key value. Customer 1 is Mina, and order 103 is hers. An order line needs both order_id and line_no : line 1 of order 103 is different from line 1 of order 101. This is a composite key , made of several columns. A foreign key requires a reference to match an existing key. Order 103’s customer_id = 1 points to Mina’s customer row; its line for P7 points to the blue mug’s product row. One customer can have many orders, and one order can have many lines and payments. Figure 1 draws those relationships and shows the resulting order. One order connects several kinds of fact PK = primary key; FK = foreign key. Values shown after order 103 is accepted. Amounts are pounds. customers 1 → many orders 1 → many order_items many → 1 products orders 1 → many payments customers customer_id · PK name 1 Mina Shah 2 Tariq Aziz 3 Edda Berg orders order_id · PK customer_id · FK status 103 1 pending order_items order_id · PK/FK line_no · PK product_id · FK quantity unit_price 103 1 P7 1 20.00 103 2 P3 2 4.50 products product_id · PK name price stock P3 Green tea, 50 g 4.50 10 P7 Blue mug 20.00 0 P9 Teapot 35.00 4 payments payment_id · PK order_id · FK amount method 501 101 30.00 card 502 101 9.50 gift card 503 102 40.00 card Figure 1. Illustrative shop data after order 103 is accepted. PK marks columns forming the primary key; FK marks a foreign key. Labels show how many rows on either side can correspond; foreign-key values identify the referenced rows. A customer can have no orders, and an order can have no lines or payments. The order and line tables show only 103; payments show earlier orders 101 and 102. Amounts are pounds. This view omits dates and historical rows, not additional stock reservations. Read this figure as text Mina Shah is customer 1. Her pending order 103 has two lines: one blue mug P7 at £20.00 and two green teas P3 at £4.50 each. Its value is £29.00 and it has no payment. Stock is now zero mugs, ten teas and four teapots. Earlier payments 501 and 502 settle order 101; 503 settles order 102. Tariq Aziz and Edda Berg retain customer identities 2 and 3. The product’s current price and the line’s agreed price are different facts. Keeping unit_price on the line preserves the £20.00 agreement even if tomorrow’s mug costs £22.00. Copying Mina’s current name onto every order would instead create several copies of one changing fact, each needing correction. The schema is the definition of tables, their values and their rules. A constraint is a rule the database checks when accepting a change. For example, an order-line quantity must be a whole number, present and positive: quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0 ) integer chooses whole numbers, NOT NULL requires a value and CHECK rejects a value failing its condition. A zero-quantity line fails even if an import bypasses the shop’s form. This does not establish that the customer ordered the quantity supplied; the application still has to send the intended facts. Designing relational data develops identity, relationships, values and the rules a schema can enforce. Ask for an answer and check its shape SQL is the language used to ask for and change rows in most relational systems. It is largely declarative : describe the result and let the engine, the software implementing the database, choose how to produce it. First say what one result row should mean. Here we want one row for order 103, with the customer’s current name and the sum of its line values. A join combines rows whose values satisfy a condition. SELECT names output values, FROM names an input table and WHERE filters rows by a condition. The query below matches each order line to its order and each order to its customer. SUM adds the line values; GROUP BY combines the matched rows into one result per order and customer name. SELECT o.order_id, c.name, SUM (i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_value FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_id = 103 GROUP BY o.order_id, c.name; PostgreSQL returned 103 | Mina Shah | 29.00 : £20.00 + 2 × £4.50. The short names o , c and i label the input tables. Matching a line to its one customer did not multiply that line. Adding another independent detail table can. Order 101 has two lines, £4.50 and £35.00, and two payments, £30.00 and £9.50. Both totals should be £39.50. Join lines directly to payments by order, however, and each line matches both payments: Order 101 · join each line to each payment line_no Line value (£) payment_id amount (£) 1 4.50 501 30.00 1 4.50 502 9.50 2 35.00 501 30.00 2 35.00 502 9.50 Figure 2. Illustrative joined rows, checked against PostgreSQL. Each line and each payment appears twice: summing either amount column gives £79.00. This is an intermediate query result, not four stored order lines. The example includes only order 101, whose lines and payments are both present. The wrong query returns £79.00 ordered and £79.00 paid. Its balance is zero, accidentally correct, so checking the balance alone misses the error. Check the contributing totals and the identity represented by each row. The wrong join, and the repair SELECT SUM (i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_value, SUM (p.amount) AS paid FROM order_items AS i JOIN payments AS p ON p.order_id = i.order_id WHERE i.order_id = 101 ; SELECT l.order_value, p.paid FROM ( SELECT order_id, SUM (quantity * unit_price) AS order_value FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id ) AS l JOIN ( SELECT order_id, SUM (amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id ) AS p ON p.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.order_id = 101 ; The repair totals lines and payments separately, each producing one row per order, then joins those totals. It returns £39.50 and £39.50. Order 103 has no payment, so this particular inner join, which keeps only matching rows, would omit it. A report of money still due must deliberately retain unpaid orders. Working with SQL develops an unpaid-order report in its own resettable fixture, then missing values, ordering and checked changes. Correctness comes before speed: making this query faster would leave its question wrong. Reserve the last mug Rewind to just before order 103. Stock is one mug and twelve teas. Accepting the pending order reserves its items now; taking payment happens later. Our rule is that the shop must not accept more new mug commitments than the stock available. Cancellation and payment failure would need a later protocol to release or complete a reservation. A transaction groups database work into a change that is kept or discarded as a unit. BEGIN starts it, COMMIT asks to keep it and ROLLBACK discards it. Keeping all its database changes or none is atomicity . Mina must not lose stock if writing her order fails, or gain an order if reserving either product fails. Atomicity alone does not settle competing decisions. Suppose both buyers read stock 1, calculate 0 in their applications, then write that calculated 0 and their orders. Both transactions can commit. Stock is non-negative, but two customers have been promised one mug. The quantity checks and foreign keys all pass. Isolation specifies how overlapping transactions may see and affect one another. At PostgreSQL’s default setting, Read Committed , an ordinary query reads changes committed before that query began. A later update does not automatically invalidate an earlier application decision. Figure 3 compares the stale assignment with a change that checks availability as it subtracts. Who gets the last blue mug? Stock change Read, calculate, write Conditional subtraction One mug Mina · order 103 Not started Tariq · order 104 Not started Committed state · product P7 stock Accepted new orders 1 None Neither customer has an accepted new order. Play Back Next Reset 1 / 5 Figure 3. Illustrative PostgreSQL Read Committed histories, verified on a native server with competing buyers. One blue mug is available before order 103. Both options use transactions; only the conditional option rechecks availability when it changes stock. The display shows committed stock, so Mina’s uncommitted subtraction is described in her lane. Tea and order writes are omitted from the picture; the accompanying protocol includes them. No payment or cancellation occurs during either history. Underlined values changed at this step. Read this figure as text With an earlier read followed by a calculated assignment, both customers read 1 and later write 0. Both orders commit: two mugs sold, stock 0. With conditional subtraction, Mina changes the row first. Tariq waits, then rechecks against 0 after Mina commits. He changes zero rows and rolls back. Only order 103 is accepted. The repaired update says “subtract one only if at least one remains”. A competing updater of P7 waits for the first transaction; after its commit, PostgreSQL rechecks the condition against the changed row. Tariq finds zero available and changes zero rows. His application must treat that result as refusal and roll back, rather than insert order 104 anyway. Here is Mina’s complete database path for this new order. The comments describe required application branches; they are not SQL instructions that perform those branches. Every stock-taking writer must use the guarded subtraction, and both returned-row checks must pass before proceeding. This example fixes identifiers, prices and quantities to make the protocol visible. BEGIN ; UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = 'P7' AND stock >= 1 RETURNING stock; -- Application: require one returned row, otherwise ROLLBACK. UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 2 WHERE product_id = 'P3' AND stock >= 2 RETURNING stock; -- Application: require one returned row, otherwise ROLLBACK. INSERT INTO orders VALUES ( 103 , 1 , '2026-10-20 10:15+00' , 'pending' ); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES ( 103 , 1 , 'P7' , 1 , 20 . 00 ), ( 103 , 2 , 'P3' , 2 , 4 . 50 ); COMMIT ; -- Application: ROLLBACK on any error; confirm only after COMMIT succeeds. If the mug or tea is unavailable, rollback discards the whole attempt, including any earlier subtraction. Any statement error must also lead to rollback. On success, stock becomes P7 0 and P3 10, and order 103 has both lines. A lost commit reply needs a further application rule, below. This argument covers a condition on one product row at a time. Rules involving counts across several rows need a broader protocol. Different engines and isolation settings also permit different histories. Making concurrent changes correct develops those choices and how to test the forbidden outcomes. Merely wrapping an arbitrary sequence in BEGIN and COMMIT does not prove it safe. Follow the work behind the statement The same SQL result can require very different work. A scan examines table rows to find matches. An index is an additional structure that helps locate rows by selected values. P7’s primary-key index gives PostgreSQL a route to its product row; on a tiny three-row table the engine may reasonably choose a scan instead. Stored rows occupy pages , blocks read into memory together. PostgreSQL normally uses 8 KiB pages. Its cache holds copies of those pages so repeated work can avoid loading them again. An update changes a row in memory and records enough information to recover the change. Find P7. Choose a scan or an index route to the product row. Change in memory. Check stock and subtract; another updater may wait here. Make the commit recoverable. Record changes in a write-ahead log (WAL), a history from which the engine can reconstruct them. With ordinary durable settings, flush the commit’s log records to storage before confirming success. Write data pages. Changed pages can reach their table files later. Crash recovery can replay the stored log if needed. Figure 4. Illustrative PostgreSQL write path, based on its documented storage and log contract. It omits index maintenance, background work and detailed row versions; it is not a measured timeline. The underlying storage must honour its durability promises. Durability is the promise that an acknowledged commit survives the failures covered by that configuration. It does not require every changed data page to be written before the acknowledgement. Relaxing the commit’s wait for storage changes what a crash may lose; losing the whole storage device requires another copy. A single-order lookup should ideally touch little data. A report adding every order’s value may need most of the order lines even when it returns one total. An index adds storage and work to changes, so creating one for every column is costly. PostgreSQL’s EXPLAIN shows its chosen execution plan, the operations used to answer a statement; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it and reports observations. Start a slow-request investigation by separating time spent waiting to reach the database, executing work, waiting behind another transaction and transferring results. Then inspect the responsible statements. Understanding and improving database performance follows that evidence through storage, indexes, plans and concurrent load. Complete the application request Order 103 commits, but the reply to Mina’s browser is lost. The database has an order; Mina sees a timeout. If the database’s own commit reply is lost, even the application may be uncertain whether the order committed. A timeout reports the end of a wait, not the absence of a change. Give this logical order attempt a stable identity before sending it. On repetition, reuse that identity and recover or coordinate the same result. Here order 103 can identify the attempt, provided it is assigned before the first attempt and tied to the same customer and items. Its primary key rejects a second order 103; that rejection alone does not return the original result or verify that the repeated input matches. The application needs a complete outcome-resolution protocol, especially while the first attempt could still commit. Generating a fresh order identifier because the reply was lost would instead start another order. Keep Tariq’s losing 104 distinct from Mina’s repeated 103. External fulfilment has another boundary. A database rollback cannot recall an ordinary request already accepted by a parcel service. Record the work to do with the order in the same transaction, then let a worker perform it with its own recovery rules. Building applications around a relational database develops safe request replay, external work and bounded use of connections, the channels carrying application–database exchanges. The contract also changes as the application evolves. Suppose the shop adds a delivery country. A new application cannot assume every old order has one as soon as the column exists. Old writers may still omit it. First add a representation old code can use, update writers, fill existing rows using justified values, verify completeness, then require the value. Changing a live database owns that compatibility sequence and its interruption plan. A schema change is unfinished while live applications disagree about its meaning. Recover the right state At 10:10 on 20 October, a mistaken clean-up deletes paid order 101 with its lines and payments. Order 103 is validly placed at 10:15. The database has faithfully committed the mistake. Three recovery mechanisms answer different questions: Crash recovery Bring the same database back after interrupted execution, preserving its committed work. It keeps the committed deletion. Replica failover Make another maintained copy, a replica, serve in place of a failed writer. A replica that has copied the deletion is missing 101 too. Restore an earlier state Reconstruct data from retained recovery inputs. PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery uses a base backup, a recoverable starting copy, plus saved log history, stopping before the mistake. Restoring to 10:09 recovers order 101 but predates valid order 103. Restore separately first, compare the histories and decide how to repair affected facts while accounting for later orders and external work. Replacing today’s whole database with yesterday’s correct copy can discard today’s correct purchases. Give the service a named operating owner and explicit targets. An illustrative shop policy might allow five minutes of data loss after losing its location and require usable service within an hour. These are requirements, not measured results. A restore rehearsal must time retrieval, reconstruction, validation and application reconnection, then check known orders and their relationships. A successful backup job has not performed that rehearsal. Access control, which limits who can read or change data, and health observations are part of this responsibility. A managed service takes specified operating duties; the shop still needs an owner for its data and recovery acceptance. Running a relational service develops those duties, the failure-specific targets and the recovery gates. Put data and decisions in the right place Suppose the application writes order 103 to one server, then immediately reads it from a replica that has not applied the change yet. The answer is “no such order” even though the write succeeded. Replication maintains copies of data; its timing determines how fresh each copy’s answers can be. Keep this immediate read on the writer, or use a supported way to wait for the replica to include the write. Copying data does not divide its write ownership. Several read replicas can help suitable reporting reads, but ordinary changes to the same P7 stock still meet at the writer. A concrete reason to divide ownership would be measured write demand for independent product ranges exceeding one suitably tuned server’s capacity. Sharding assigns different subsets of data to different write owners. Splitting products can spread those independent changes, but Mina’s mug-and-tea order might now cross owners. Either a distributed transaction coordinates an all-or-nothing change across them, or the application must adopt different rules for accepting and repairing partly completed work. Location, routing and what happens when an owner cannot be reached become application-visible decisions. A distributed relational system supplies some of that coordination within the database product. It still has a documented failure and freshness contract, communication delays and placement choices to test. Start with a demonstrated need for divided ownership or failure survival. The existing operating discussion of replicas and partitions supplies the next questions; Choosing a relational database compares deployment boundaries. Choose a system you can test Choose an engine and an arrangement for running it together. Consider an illustrative shop with three application hosts sharing the same stock, a team able to operate one managed database service, and no demonstrated need for writes in several regions. Compare three shapes: Embedded · SQLite The engine runs inside an application process and owns local files. It suits a single-device shop or local application. Directly sharing one SQLite WAL database between these three hosts fails its same-host access requirement. Placing SQLite behind one application service changes the candidate and leaves that service’s recovery to prove. Conventional server · PostgreSQL Applications share a database service through connections. Shortlist a managed PostgreSQL deployment for this shop, subject to the tests below. A single local server, including our verification server, does not establish survival of host loss. Distributed relational service Keep conditional on a demonstrated need to spread ownership or survive a specified wider failure while working. Compare placement, transaction delays and operational cost against a server arrangement meeting the same requirements. The current conclusion is a starting shortlist, not production acceptance. The first candidate is PostgreSQL because shared relational changes fit the application and a managed service fits the stated operating capacity. Disqualify it if the selected deployment fails a hard requirement. Keep each piece of evidence labelled: a manual documents a promise, a run measures one arrangement, and a forecast remains an assumption. What would make this shortlist defensible? Requirement Evidence to obtain Facts and query meaning Run the schema and critical queries; verify exact prices, missing values and relationship checks in the chosen engine. Competing changes and durable acknowledgement Race for the last mug and interrupt requests. Verify accepted identities after the failure the deployment claims to survive. Use transactions and application recovery . Workload, volume and geography Measure order-taking together with reports at forecast and burst demand, from the intended locations. Include waiting and refused work. Use performance diagnosis . Change and recovery ownership Rehearse compatible application change and an isolated restore. Record times, loss and responsible people. Use live changes and operations . Specialist features and ecosystem Check required add-on features, application-library value conversions, permissions and support in the actual managed offering. Cost, portability and exit Price the passing arrangement including copies, backups, traffic and operating effort; export and re-import representative data, checking values and rules. Record engine-specific dependencies. Change the workload and the shortlist can change. A report over years of order lines may favour a column store, which stores column values together for broad scans and calculations. The shop might keep transactional truth in PostgreSQL and feed a reporting copy, with an explicit freshness and recovery policy. A document store can suit independently changed documents; object storage suits product photographs; a search engine suits relevance-ranked discovery. Compare their actual contracts against the task, and account for maintaining another copy. Begin with a disposable prototype and a small set of rejection tests. You can practise SQL while the production choice remains open. Choosing a relational database carries the evaluation through a concrete candidate record, costs and an adoption decision. The complete draft collection is available for review. See the new draft collection . Read in context: Relational databases . Mina and Tariq can each see the last place in a class and both book it. Their requests can finish without a database error, with no negative counter and no duplicate booking identifier. The error is in the combination: the shop has promised two places when it has only one. A transaction groups database work into a change that commits together or is rolled back (discarded) together. It gives us a boundary for fixing that race, but we still have to decide what belongs inside it and how competing decisions are protected. Those choices determine whether a successful response means a booking the shop can honour. This article builds on the tables, keys and first competing buyers in Relational databases . The same shop also runs classes: remaining places play the part of product stock, and a reservation records who took a place. We will work through PostgreSQL 18, then identify where another engine needs a different argument. Finish this article before choosing a deeper article; it supplies the decisions those articles build on. Start with the fact that must remain true Two transactions can sell the same place Put the condition inside the change What a read sees, and what a lock protects Protect a decision spanning several rows When transactions wait or fail What COMMIT can promise Test the schedule that could break the rule Start with the fact that must remain true An invariant is a rule that every accepted state must satisfy. For each class, remaining places must stay between zero and capacity, and remaining + number of reservations = capacity . A customer may book a class only once. Together these rules say more than “the counter is nonnegative”: every consumed place has an owner, and nobody owns two places through two clicks. These are the starting rows. A primary key (PK) identifies a row; a foreign key (FK) refers to a row in another table. The reservation’s owner_id refers to customers: Mina is 1, Tariq 2 and Edda 3. classes class_id · PK title capacity remaining 21 Tea tasting 1 1 22 Mug painting 3 2 classes.class_id ← reservations.class_id reservations request_id · PK class_id · FK owner_id · FK R7 22 2 Tariq already holds R7 in Mug painting, so that class has two places left. Tea tasting has its last place available. Each figure restarts from these rows unless it says otherwise; they are separate experiments. Keep ownership and the counter together A booking reduces remaining and inserts a reservation. BEGIN opens an explicit transaction; successful COMMIT accepts its work, and ROLLBACK discards it. A statement is one SQL command. Without an explicit boundary, PostgreSQL normally commits each successful standalone statement. Two statements can therefore become two independent promises. Figure 1 starts with Mina booking Mug painting as R10. Her second click, R11, tries to book it again. Compare what happens when the decrement commits before the duplicate reservation is refused. Figure 1. A rejected double click must not consume a second place Illustrative model of selected PostgreSQL schedules. Protection Separate commits One transaction Mina’s request Mina’s second request Committed classes class_id · PK capacity remaining 22 3 2 classes.class_id ← reservations.class_id Committed reservations request_id · PK class_id · FK owner_id · FK Play Back Next Reset The tables show committed state; the lanes describe pending work. Fixed steps omit timing, storage and other requests. This figure runs a model, not a database. Read this figure as text Starting from class 22, Mina books R10, then her second request R11 fails the one-booking-per-customer rule. Separate commits leave remaining = 0 with two reservations for capacity 3. One transaction rolls back the second decrement: remaining = 1 and two reservations. With one transaction, the failed second booking loses its decrement too. This all-or-nothing property is atomicity . Keep the whole invariant-changing operation inside that boundary. For a move, releasing the old place and taking the new one belong together; two commits can lose the original booking without acquiring its replacement. A savepoint marks a place within a transaction to which some work can be rolled back. It is not a separate commit. Rolling back only the failed insert while retaining its decrement would recreate the broken state. Transactional behaviour also has exceptions: PostgreSQL’s number-generating sequences do not give back consumed numbers on rollback. Check commands that change table definitions and number generation against the engine rather than treating all effects as ordinary rows. Give the database the rules it can enforce A constraint is a rule the database checks when storing a change. CHECK (remaining BETWEEN 0 AND capacity) , with non-null columns, rejects an impossible counter. UNIQUE (class_id, owner_id) rejects the second booking even when two requests both checked and found no earlier one. The primary key on request_id prevents two reservations sharing that identifier, and foreign keys reject unknown classes and customers. The equality between remaining places and reservation count spans tables. PostgreSQL cannot enforce it with a CHECK on the class row. The transaction protocol must preserve it on every path: ordinary booking, cancellation, move, capacity change and staff import. This is the consistency in ACID : atomicity, consistency, isolation (the contract for overlapping work) and durability (survival after commit). Constraints and correct application logic supply the rules; the database cannot infer that a decrement needs a reservation. Two transactions can sell the same place Return to Tea tasting. Mina asks for R8 and Tariq for R9. Each first reads remaining = 1 , calculates 1 − 1 = 0 , then writes that calculated zero and inserts its reservation. Each transaction preserves the rule when run alone from the starting state. We use PostgreSQL’s Read Committed setting: ordinary queries see committed data as each command begins. -- A and B have both read remaining = 1. BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED ; UPDATE classes SET remaining = 0 WHERE class_id = 21 ; INSERT INTO reservations (request_id, class_id, owner_id) VALUES ( 'R8' , 21 , 1 ); -- B uses ('R9', 21, 2) COMMIT ; The important question is whether the read still authorises the write. Step through Figure 2 with Read, then overwrite . Its lanes are a schedule : a chosen order of reads, writes and commits across independent transactions. The tables show the committed state, separate from pending work in each lane. Figure 2. Two requests, one place: where does the condition run? Illustrative model of selected PostgreSQL schedules. Protection Read, then overwrite Conditional change Mina’s request Tariq’s request Committed classes class_id · PK capacity remaining 21 1 1 classes.class_id ← reservations.class_id Committed reservations request_id · PK class_id · FK owner_id · FK Play Back Next Reset The tables show committed state; the lanes describe pending work. Fixed steps omit timing, storage and other requests. This figure runs a model, not a database. Read this figure as text Class 21 has one place. Both requests initially read 1. With a stale overwrite, R8 and R9 both commit and remaining is 0: two bookings for one place. With a conditional change, Tariq waits for Mina, rechecks remaining > 0, changes no row and creates no R9. Both commit, leaving two reservations and zero remaining places. What a read sees, and what a lock protects A view is not ownership Isolation specifies how transactions may observe and interfere with each other. PostgreSQL keeps several row versions , the values before and after a change, so an ordinary reader can use a committed older value while a writer is working. A snapshot selects which versions that read can see. This is multiversion concurrency control , or MVCC. At Read Committed, each ordinary query gets a new snapshot. A report can read one remaining place, another transaction books it, and the report’s next query finds a reservation while still holding its earlier counter in application memory. A changed reread is a nonrepeatable read ; a changed set of matching rows is a phantom . Neither means PostgreSQL exposed uncommitted work, which would be a dirty read . A row lock holds conflicting writers or locking readers back from the selected row. An ordinary PostgreSQL read usually continues using a permitted version. Every move path taking the distinct classes in ascending order, 21 then 22, removes this particular cycle: Tariq waits before holding 22, leaving Mina able to finish.
